planting.note: Set rooted semi-hardwood cuttings in spring into pure, deep, well-drained sand in full sun; seed set is unreliable in cultivation so nursery stock is propagated almost entirely from cuttings.

directions: Plant container-grown nursery stock in full sun in deep, sterile-looking white or yellow sand with sharp drainage, avoiding any site that holds moisture after rain. Garberia is a Florida Central Ridge scrub and sandhill endemic shrub with resinous, gray-green, aromatic leaves and showy heads of pink-lavender disc flowers (no ray florets) that open in October and November, a critical late nectar source for migrating monarchs and native scrub bees. It needs no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established and will decline quickly in rich or poorly drained soil. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain a dense, rounded habit; otherwise plants are low-maintenance once sited correctly.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Direct sow or set transplants in spring into lean, deep, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; established plants resent transplanting once their taproot develops.

directions: Sow seed on the surface of dry, infertile, deep sand in full sun, or set out young transplants in spring, siting plants where their long taproot will never sit in standing water. Feay's Palafox is a woody-based Florida scrub endemic reaching 3 to 6 feet, with narrow gray-green leaves and loose clusters of rayless, rose-pink disc flowers from late summer into fall that draw native bees and skippers. It thrives on neglect in pure scrub sand and is intolerant of fertilizer, mulch buildup, or irrigation beyond establishment. Cut back lightly in late winter to keep the open, airy habit tidy for small-space scrub gardens.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat before sowing directly into dry, lean, deep sand in full sun; germination improves noticeably after scarification.

directions: Scarify the hard-coated seed and sow into dry, deep, infertile sand in full sun, or divide established clumps in spring. Alicia is a low, wiry-stemmed perennial in the pea family endemic to Florida sandhill and scrub, with fine pinnately compound leaflets and small clusters of yellow, pea-shaped flowers produced nearly year-round in mild winters. It is extremely drought-tolerant once rooted and fixes its own nitrogen, so it needs no fertilizer and performs best when left alone in open, sunny sand. Use it as a low-growing filler among taller scrub shrubs or along sandy path edges where little else will persist.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or set small container plants in spring into dry, acidic, deep sand in full sun; seed germinates slowly and unevenly so most nursery stock is grown from cuttings.

directions: Plant small container stock or rooted cuttings in full sun in dry, acidic, deep sandy soil with no amendment, spacing plants to form a loose groundcover along open sandhill edges or dry xeric borders. This low, wiry, evergreen subshrub of longleaf pine sandhills and scrub from the Carolinas to Florida and the Gulf Coast has tiny needle-like leaves and bright yellow, five-petaled flowers in late spring and early summer that attract small native bees. It is highly drought- and fire-adapted, resprouting readily from the base after prescribed burns or mowing, and declines if soil stays consistently moist or fertile. Shear lightly after bloom only if a tighter mat is wanted; otherwise it needs no routine maintenance.
sources: Weakley's Flora of the Southeastern United States

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns directly in fall shortly after they drop, 1 to 2 inches deep in deep, well-drained sand; like other white oaks, acorns have no hard dormancy and should not be allowed to dry out before planting.

directions: Sow fresh fall-collected acorns promptly in deep, well-drained sandy soil in full sun, or plant young container or bare-root stock while small, since this oak forms a long taproot early and transplants poorly once established. Sand post oak is a small, often shrubby deciduous tree of the deep-sand longleaf pine sandhills and scrub of the southeastern Coastal Plain, closely related to post oak but shorter and more drought-adapted, with lobed, cross-shaped leaves and a gnarled, wind-sculpted form. It is extremely drought- and fire-tolerant, resprouting from the root crown after burns, and is a valuable wildlife tree whose acorns feed deer, turkey, and small mammals. Site it only in sharply drained, infertile sand in full sun, where it will grow slowly into a long-lived, picturesque specimen requiring no irrigation or fertilizer.
sources: Weakley's Flora of the Southeastern United States

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, dry to moderately moist, acidic sandy soil in full sun; plants form a basal rosette the first year and flower in subsequent seasons.

directions: Direct sow seed or set transplants into dry, lean, acidic sandy soil in full sun; this longleaf pine sandhill and flatwoods native from North Carolina to Florida and Louisiana forms a basal rosette of broad, strap-shaped leaves that release a sweet vanilla-like fragrance (from coumarin) when dried, historically harvested as a tobacco and sachet flavoring. From late summer through fall it sends up upright stems topped with flat-topped clusters of lavender-purple composite flowers that are highly attractive to migrating monarchs, native bees, and skippers. Once established it is reliably drought-tolerant and fire-adapted, resprouting readily after prescribed burns. Avoid heavy, wet, or fertile soils, which cause rot and floppy, weak growth.
